⚡️🇩🇪🇱🇹 Reuters: Germany's army has begun its first tactical tests of kamikaze drones in Lithuania, along with Helsing's AI based targeting software Clarity. The drone tests took place on Sunday during Freedom Shield, Germany's largest military drills in the country to date.
Army chief Lieutenant General Christian Freuding watched loitering munitions made by German companies Helsing and Stark, fitted with inert warheads, hit main battle tanks at the Rudninkai training ground near the Belarusian border. Days earlier, troops there tested Clarity, which processes data from satellites, drones and other sensors and recommends actions to commanders. Freuding described both kinds of systems as essential to modern warfare.
Germany only decided in 2025 to buy loitering munitions. An armoured brigade of 5,000 German troops will be stationed permanently in Lithuania by the end of 2027, with about 1,800 already deployed there.

🇵🇭 Philippines prepares new US military access point near Taiwan 
The Philippines -[ a platform for an expanding US military presence in the region](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73756) amid its political standoff with China - is about to upgrade an airport in the northernmost province of Batanes, reports Bloomberg.
🔴 Basco Airport on Batan Island lies less than 200 km from Taiwan, placing it close to a potential flashpoint in a US-China standoff
🔴 the airport currently has a short runway and cannot operate in all weather conditions, limiting aircraft access
🔴 it will receive infrastructure improvements to accommodate larger aircraft 
🔴 upgrade is intended to improve US-Philippine military access, disaster response and commercial supply routes
The initiative forms part of a broader push to deepen military cooperation.
Under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA), the US has expanded the number of designated military sites in the country from five to nine since 2022, alongside increasingly frequent joint exercises.
The move also aligns with new US Army operational [warfighting guidance released in October](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76428?single), that calls for stronger command facilities, logistics networks and ammunition stockpiles to ensure American forces can deploy rapidly in a potential conflict.
China has repeatedly warned that [expanding military deployments and joint drills in the region](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71601) risk destabilizing the Asia-Pacific and escalating tensions.

events.text:
🇯🇵 What’s steering Japan’s carmakers toward massive rearmament drive?
The Japanese government is encouraging the country’s automakers to join its biggest military buildup since World War II, Reuters reports.
👉 Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi believes that tapping into existing industrial supply chains will accelerate Japan’s rearmament, which is gathering pace with US backing.
One striking example is Japanese manufacturer Aster, which previously supplied components for Toyota vehicles. The company has since carved out a new niche supplying electric motors for[ lethal drones developed by US defense technology company Anduril .](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/78025)
➡️ Japan’s new military doctrine justifies ramping up defense spending by pointing to alleged security “threats” from North Korea, China and Russia. But China’s daily, the Global Times, has pushed back against the strategy as a form of “military Keynesianism” – employing defense spending to pump up broader economic growth. Interestingly, Germany appears to be following a similar path, increasingly redirecting[ its automotive industry towards military production.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/77897)
The problem, however, is that this strategy may not deliver the promised economic benefits. Japan faces competing demands for public spending, while Takaichi has yet to explain how she would fund further hikes in military expenditures without placing an even greater strain on the country’s already stretched public finances, Reuters argued last August.
The Chinese media have warned that Japan is going down the same road it took prior to World War II – one that brought catastrophe to the region. Meanwhile, Beijing is tightening its rare-earth supplies to Japan, potentially throwing another obstacle in the way of [Tokyo’s military buildup. ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72149)
🔊 Some observers have also drawn a parallel between Germany’s and Japan’s escalating defense budgets, seeing echoes of the geopolitical climate that preceded World War II. For them, this may point to a broader geopolitical project to remilitarize both countries.
Remarkably, in April, America’s leading technology company,[ Palantir, which has close ties to the CIA and the Pentagon](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/68441), published a manifesto calling for precisely such a shift. It stated explicitly that the postwar neutering of Germany and Japan must be undone.
👍 [Substack](https://geopoliticsprime.substack.com/) | [Chat](https://t.me/+HLrnOk92f31mYzIy) |

events.title: Telegram
events.text:
🇦🇪 UAE granted Israel backdoor F-16 access to secure US arms deal - book
The UAE granted Israel access to software running its most advanced F-16 fighter jets in the late 1990s in exchange for Tel Aviv dropping it's opposition to a major US arms sale to the country, according to investigative journalist Matthew Cole's book “Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East.”
Mohamed bin Zayed, then chief of staff of the UAE Armed Forces, was seeking to acquire 80 F-16 Block 60 fighters, according to an excerpt shared on X by journalist Murtaza Hussain.
The deal faced a major obstacle: the US’ longstanding commitment to ensuring Israel maintained a “qualitative military edge” over its Arab neighbors.
♦️ the UAE offered to buy and install Israeli software on its new F-16s, effectively giving Israeli systems access to the aircraft's operations
♦️ “no Muslim nation had ever made such an offer before,” per Cole 
 
♦️ the US reportedly facilitated secret negotiations between Emirati and Israeli representatives to overcome resistance to the sale
♦️ Lockheed Martin ultimately delivered the fighters, while Israel supplied and installed the software
The UAE announced the planned purchase during a May 1998 visit to Washington. The formal US notification to Congress followed on April 27, 2000, putting the deal's value at $6.43 billion.
The account places covert UAE-Israeli military cooperation more than two decades before the 2020 Abraham Accords formally normalized relations between the two countries.
